title: Humic Substances and Plant Growth-Promoting Microorganisms for Sustainable Crop Production: Mechanisms, Evidence Gaps, and Ecological Safety
content: Humic substances (HSs) and plant growth-promoting microorganisms (PGPMs) are promising inputs for sustainable crop production, yet the efficacy and ecological safety of their co-application remain uncertain. This review synthesizes evidence on individual and combined applications, focusing on mechanisms, context-dependent outcomes, knowledge gaps, and research priorities. HSs influence nutrient availability, rhizosphere chemistry, and plant physiology, whereas PGPMs support nutrient mobilization, nitrogen fixation, hormonal regulation, and pathogen suppression. Combined treatments have improved growth and nutrient acquisition in maize and soybean, including soybean performance under water deficit in salt-affected soil. However, the absence of significant growth enhancement during orchid acclimatization highlights variable responses. Outcomes depend on HS composition and dose, microbial identity, crop species, environmental conditions, and application method. Evidence remains limited for combined biocontrol, interactions involving mycorrhizal fungi, and long-term effects on native microbial communities. Co-application benefits do not establish synergy without appropriate comparisons with individual treatments, and agronomic improvements do not demonstrate ecological safety. Standardized multifactorial experiments, long-term field validation, and formulation-specific safety assessments, supported by multi-omics and ecological modeling, are needed to guide effective and environmentally responsible HS–PGPM use.
